findings: User.ts declares `phone: string` as required/non-null, but schema.sql defines `phone TEXT NULL`. listActiveUsers() in userRepo.ts does `SELECT id, email, phone FROM users` and casts the result to `Promise<User[]>` with no null-check or COALESCE — any row with a NULL phone will silently violate the type contract, so downstream code that trusts `user.phone` as a string (e.g. calling `.toUpperCase()` or formatting it) will throw or misbehave at runtime for exactly the rows the schema says are legal.

listActiveUsers() is named as if it filters soft-deleted users (the schema has `deleted_at TIMESTAMP NULL` for exactly this purpose) but its query `SELECT id, email, phone FROM users` has no `WHERE deleted_at IS NULL` clause. It returns every user including soft-deleted ones, contradicting its own name/contract — any caller (e.g. an admin panel, a mailing list, or an active-user count) will silently include deleted accounts.

signup() enforces 'no duplicate email' via a check-then-insert pattern (`SELECT id ... WHERE email=$1` followed by a separate `INSERT`) with no transaction, locking, or advisory lock, and schema.sql explicitly notes 'no UNIQUE constraint on email'. Two concurrent signup calls with the same email can both pass the SELECT (finding zero rows) before either INSERT commits, producing two rows with the same email — the 'email taken' invariant is not actually enforced under concurrency, and there is no DB-level backstop since the column isn't UNIQUE.

The duplicate-email check in signup() (`SELECT id FROM users WHERE email=$1`) does not exclude soft-deleted rows (`deleted_at IS NOT NULL`), so once a user is soft-deleted their email permanently blocks any new signup with that same address — a legitimate user who deletes their account (or is deleted by an admin) can never re-register with the same email, since the existence check treats deleted and active rows identically.
